share of participants had posteriors pressed against the upper bound: 59% had
their 97.5% credible limit pinned at 0.35, and 68% had posterior means above

latent state switches on roughly every third trial — far more often than the
true switch rate (~0.05 per trial; episodes are 16–24 trials long). This was
implausible on its face and motivated a systematic investigation rather than
simply accepting the values or extending the bound further.

The h_switch–noise_reactivity coupling is genuine, not an artefact

children.label: The h_switch–noise_reactivity coupling is genuine, not an artefact

children.value:
are positively
correlated (r = +0.60). This is theoretically expected: a person who perceives
the environment as more volatile (high

) and simultaneously attributes
surprising outcomes more readily to genuine change rather than noise is
expressing a coherent, correlated cognitive style. Because the two parameters
sit on either side of the same switch threshold, a positive association across
individuals is exactly what the volatility/stochasticity framework predicts.
A coupling of this kind could, in principle, also arise as an

— if the network compressed the two parameters along the threshold
line. We tested this directly. In simulation,
; if the inference induced a spurious coupling, the

parameters would correlate despite the independent ground truth.
They do not: the estimated correlation is ≈ 0 (and slightly negative), while the
real-participant correlation is strongly positive.

children.alt:
Left: simulated data with noise_reactivity and h_switch drawn
independently. The estimated parameters show no spurious correlation
(estimated r ≈ 0), confirming the inference does not manufacture coupling.
Right: real participants. The posteriors show a clear positive coupling
(r = +0.60), and all participants lie above the single-oddball switch threshold
h = 0.1 \cdot nr (dashed line) — i.e. they reliably treat oddballs as state
switches. The coupling is therefore a genuine psychological effect.

Because the simulated check rules out an inference-induced artefact, the
correlation observed in the real data reflects genuine individual differences in
cognitive style. This is a substantive finding rather than a nuisance, and it is
consistent with the prior theoretical expectation that perceived volatility and
the propensity to attribute change (rather than noise) covary.
